title: NC: Hammering The Teaching Profession
author: Peter Greene
summary: Greene examines North Carolina's new teacher licensure blueprint, produced by a commission he argues is a front for SAS and the Southern Regional Education Board. After a catalogue of the state's decade of hostility to public education, he translates the blueprint's ten vague actions, arguing the end game is an outcomes-based licensure and pay system tied to test scores and value-added modelling. His reading is that the plan lowers entry bars, standardizes teaching, and makes the profession cheaper to fill rather than more attractive. He closes by urging teachers to flood the State Board with email.
points: The licensure blueprint's vague language hides an outcomes-based, test-score-driven merit system for teachers.
The commission was allegedly a front, with vendors such as SAS standing to profit from value-added measurement.
Adding rungs to the career ladder may only lower the bottom while enabling alternative entry routes.
Standardizing teaching into paint-by-numbers makes the profession easier and cheaper to staff, not more appealing.
North Carolina's record on funding and pay makes promises of better compensation hard to believe.
quotes: In other words, a teacher merit pay system. Not a merit pay bonus system, but an entire teacher pay system based on "merit.

That's in keeping with the plan developed by the PR firm hired to new revamped system, and the understanding of PEPSC and its friends, which is that if word of the specifics of this plan get out, and teachers hate it enough to rise up in protest, the plan will be seriously hampered, if not outright killed.

Any time someone talks about adding steps on the professional ladder, the question you have to ask is--will they add rungs above the ones we have, or are they going to dig a hole and lower the bottom end of the ladder.
Remember, this whole thing is backed by SAS, the people who invented value-added test crap (EVAAS, PVAAS, etc), a system that has been largely debunked and even thrown out in court.
I suspect what you can find are people who believe that a system like this will make teaching positions easier and cheaper to fill.
This is not a plan that will serve anyone well, least of all the students of North Carolina, and no amount of flowery argle bargle and secret meeting and general misdirection is going to change that.
